answer.evidence: The stair is drawn as a stack of repeating steps. Each step has a 1-row light edge line, then a 4-row grey tread band (rows 1-4, 9-12, 17-20, and so on). Below the tread comes a 2-row darker riser and a 1-row dark shadow line (rows 5-7, 13-15, and so on). The tread bands are separated by dark shadow rows, so each reads as a horizontal surface with its own front edge and front face. The left dirt and right sand strips are vertical cliff flanks, not receding side faces. The cobble ground from row 48 down is separate terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 9 visible tones per 16x16 tile, above the paving reference (7) and the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references. Only 17% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean brown or grey-green. They read as dark tones of the neighbouring wood and stone, not a black sticker line. The stone treads show a highlight lip, a light face, a mid tone and a dark under-edge. The cobble base below matches the paving reference in grain and per-stone shading. The wooden side posts are the weakest part, with only about 3 steps and little grain, and the total palette is small (14 colours). Even so, the piece is not thinner or flatter than the paving reference, and a careful artist would accept it beside it.
